overview.title: Surface ocean alkalinity · HighresTA
overview.heading: Surface ocean total alkalinity at 8-day, 0.25° resolution
overview.intro: HighresTA is a global reconstruction of surface total alkalinity (TA) on the OceanSODA-ETHZv2 grid. It is trained on 30,193 near-surface bottle measurements from GLODAPv2.2023 and CARIMED (583 cruises, 1982–2021), collocated with gridded salinity, temperature, sea-surface height, chlorophyll, nutrients and bottom depth. Every grid cell carries a median estimate, a 10–90 % quantile range and the ensemble spread, so TA uncertainty can be propagated into carbonate-system calculations.

model.heading: How the model works
model.intro: TA is close to conservative with salinity, so the model is a linear salinity fit plus a gradient-boosted correction, trained as a quantile ensemble.
model.equation: TA = (β₀ + β₁·S) + f(S, T, SSH, Chl, NO₃, PO₄, Si, depth, position)

items.title: Linear salinity baseline
items.text: A first-order fit of TA on salinity captures dilution and evaporation, which set most of the surface TA variability.

items.title: Gradient-boosted residual
items.text: CatBoost predicts what salinity leaves unexplained (calcification, upwelling, river input) from temperature, sea-surface height, chlorophyll, nitrate, phosphate, silicate, bottom depth and position.

items.title: Quantile ensemble
items.text: 42 members each predict the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile: 6 cruise-wise data splits × 7 near-optimal hyperparameter sets. Their spread separates into a data-split and a model-choice term.

items.title: Held-out cruises
items.text: One block of 78 cruises (4,314 samples) is never used for training or tuning by any member and gives the reported scores.

hero.lead: A gradient-boosted quantile model learns total alkalinity (TA) from bottle samples. The current design trains **42 models: 6 data splits × 7 diverse near-optimal trials**, selected from one hyperparameter study per split. Their disagreement measures sensitivity to training data, feature choices and model parameters.

sections.title: Bottle alkalinity, matched to satellite and ocean context
sections.lead: The target is total alkalinity measured on water samples. Each sample is paired with the physical and chemical state of the water at that place and time.

blocks.body: The target is **total alkalinity (TA, µmol kg⁻¹)** from near-surface bottle samples. GLODAP bottles with WOCE flag 2 are used with the cruise-level adjustments applied; CARIMED adds the Mediterranean.

blocks.title: Bottle data
rows: Global bottle TA, quality flag 2, cruise adjustments applied.
Mediterranean bottles (≤ 30 dbar, TA flag 2) from cruises not already in GLODAP.

blocks.title: Model inputs
rows: [ESA CCI SSS](https://climate.esa.int/en/projects/sea-surface-salinity/), then [SODA](https://www2.atmos.umd.edu/~ocean/), then [Copernicus Multi Observation SSS](https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/product/MULTIOBS_GLO_PHY_S_SURFACE_MYNRT_015_013/description); bottle salinity as fallback
TA is dominated by salinity; also the linear baseline.
Separates water masses that share a salinity.
Biogeochemical tracers; help resolve regional TA–salinity offsets.
Dynamic topography: a proxy for circulation and water-mass structure.
[GlobColour](https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/product/OCEANCOLOUR_GLO_BGC_L4_MY_009_104/description); ESA OC-CCI gap-filled chlorophyll stands in for the maps
Adds biological context; may be omitted by a trial.
Separates open ocean from shelf and coastal regimes.
Position on a unit sphere, so longitude 179° and −179° are neighbours.

blocks.body: All gridded predictors used for the maps come from the OceanSODA-ETHZv2 predictor pyramid.

blocks.title: Collocation
blocks.body: Bottle time and position are matched to gridded predictors in the collocation pipeline. After filtering, salinity is replaced by the first available valid value from CCI, SODA and multi-observation products, with bottle salinity as fallback. Day-of-year sine/cosine is computed during preprocessing but is not selected among the current 11 candidate features. Missing optional predictors are retained; CatBoost handles numeric missing values.

sections.title: From raw bottles to a clean training table
sections.lead: Salinity, quality flags, required values and duplicate records determine which samples enter training. Latitude and longitude are then converted to three unit-sphere coordinates.

items.name: Collocated bottles
items.body: GLODAP and CARIMED bottles matched to the gridded predictors.

items.name: TA quality
items.body: WOCE flag 2 and cruise adjustment of at most 6 µmol/kg.

items.name: Complete cases
items.body: Require TA, salinity, temperature and nitrate.

items.name: De-duplicate
items.body: Drop repeated records of the same cruise, time, position and depth.

sections.title: A linear baseline plus a boosted residual
sections.lead: TA is mostly a straight-line function of salinity. The model captures that first, then lets gradient boosting explain what is left.

items.title: 1 · Linear baseline
items.body: Ordinary least squares on salinity alone (polynomial degree 1) gives a first estimate, `TA₀(S)`.

items.title: 2 · Boosted residual
items.body: CatBoost learns the residual `TA − TA₀` using **MultiQuantile loss**, predicting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles together. Trials use the candidate features except for their selected omissions.

items.title: 3 · Prediction
items.body: The final output is `TA₀ + residual quantile`: a median estimate plus a lower and upper bound for every sample.

blocks.title: One Optuna TPE study per split: target 300 completed trials, 50 random start-up trials
rows: None, one or two non-protected features

blocks.title: Inner-CV objective and pruning
blocks.body: A trial is scored by the **median MultiQuantile validation loss over five inner folds**. After each fold, the running median is reported to a 75th-percentile pruner, with 50 start-up trials before pruning. The default is eight concurrent trials per split and two CatBoost threads per trial. SQLite studies resume until the completed-trial target is reached.

blocks.title: How the number of trees is set
blocks.body: Each inner fit trains up to **1000 trees**, with early stopping after 50 rounds. A selected member is refitted on all five training blocks using the **median best iteration count** from its trial’s inner folds, with early stopping disabled.

sections.title: 42 models from cruise-wise splits and near-optimal alternatives
sections.lead: Neighbouring bottles on one cruise are nearly identical, so a random row-wise split would leak information. The data are cut into **7 blocks of whole cruises**, balanced across salinity, and cruises are never shared across train and test. Each of the 6 splits then yields **7 models**: splits vary which cruises a model saw, members vary hyperparameters and dropped features.

blocks.body: Blocks come from a stratified, cruise-grouped k-fold (salinity quintiles; fixed seed 42). **Block 0 is the test set for all {{run.n_members|int}} models**, in every split, and is never trained on. Split k validates on block k (a different block for each split, excluded from tuning and refitting) and trains on the other five. Within those five training blocks, one Optuna study of about 300 trials is scored by leave-one-block-out cross-validation; the 7 most diverse trials within 2 % of the best loss are refitted as that split's models. 6 splits × 7 models = {{run.n_members|int}} members.

The ensemble prediction is the **mean** of the members' quantiles. All members share the same test block, so every difference between them there comes from those two sources: the data split and the model chosen within it. Individual members can be inspected and switched on or off in the selector of the next section.

blocks.title: How the 7 members of each split are selected
Selection, fallback and refitting
blocks.body: If fewer than seven trials fall within the 2% tolerance, include them all and fill the remaining places with the next-best completed trials outside it; these fill-ins are marked in metadata. Starting with the best trial, the remaining members are chosen greedily: each is the candidate furthest from its nearest selected member, where distance equally weights dropped-feature Jaccard distance and mean normalised hyperparameter distance (log-scaled where searched on a log scale). Trial selection uses inner CV only. Study seed is `100 × split`; refit seed is `100 × split + member index`. Parallel TPE searches are not exactly reproducible from the seed alone.

sections.title: Where each predictor moves the estimate
sections.lead: Nudge one predictor up and down in every ocean cell, hold the others fixed, and see how much the ensemble's median estimate changes. Salinity dominates everywhere. The other predictors make small, regional corrections.

blocks.body: Each predictor is shifted by **±δ**, a quarter of its robust spread in the training bottles (δ = 0.38 for salinity, 3.5 °C for temperature, 0.77 µmol kg⁻¹ for nitrate). For every member, the change in Q50 over that step gives a local slope in µmol kg⁻¹ per +δ. The maps show the median over models, averaged over four seasonal dates in 2019 on a 1° grid. Members that dropped a predictor during tuning are left out of its map rather than counted as zero.

blocks.note: Colour: change in median alkalinity (µmol kg⁻¹) for a +δ step, ordered by average effect; each map has its own scale. Pale cells: fewer than 80% of models agree on the direction. Hover or tap a map to read values; the ring marks the same place on every map.

ui.aria: Change in alkalinity for a step in {name}

items.title: Salinity
items.body: +15.5 µmol kg⁻¹ per +0.38 (about 41 per unit salinity) in the median cell. Members agree on the sign in 97% of ocean cells.

items.title: Nutrients, temperature, sea level
items.body: Area-weighted mean effects of 0.7–2.6 µmol kg⁻¹ per +δ, largest at high northern latitudes and in the Indo-Pacific. Members agree on the sign in only 45–61% of cells.

items.title: Depth and chlorophyll
items.body: Bottom depth matters mainly on shelves and in the Arctic. Chlorophyll has the smallest effect (0.4 µmol kg⁻¹ per +δ). Only 25 and 22 of the 42 members use them, respectively.

blocks.title: How to read these maps
blocks.body: These are one-at-a-time, local responses. Correlated predictors such as temperature and nutrients cannot change independently in the real ocean, so a single map is not a causal effect. The out-of-range flag checks each predictor separately and does not catch combinations the training data never saw. Boosted trees are flat outside the training range, so where the tooltip reports a step outside training, the response tends towards zero by construction.

sections.title: What adds up to each estimate
sections.lead: SHAP splits every prediction into one contribution per predictor. Salinity carries most of it. Location comes second, and the largest interaction is between salinity and location.

blocks.body: For one bottle or one ocean cell, the median estimate equals a **base value** plus one **contribution** per predictor (SHAP values, computed for each of the 42 members and averaged). The base value is the average estimate over the bottles shown, 2282.9 µmol kg⁻¹. A contribution of +10 means that predictor pushes the estimate 10 µmol kg⁻¹ above that average. Salinity includes the linear baseline as well as its share of the boosted residual. **Location** is the sum of the three spherical coordinates (`ncoord_x`, `ncoord_y`, `ncoord_z`), which together say where on the globe a point is.

blocks.note: Each dot is one bottle (1 500 of 4 000 random bottles explained, 1982–2021); rows are ordered by mean |contribution|, shown at the right. Red dots are high values of the predictor, blue low, relative to all bottles. Grey: location, which has no single value, or a missing predictor. Hover or tap a dot to read it. "Zoom in" narrows the axis so the small predictors can be read; dots beyond the axis are drawn at its edge.

ui.title: Contribution of each predictor to the median estimate
ui.aria: Beeswarm of the contribution of each predictor to the median alkalinity estimate

blocks.body: Mean absolute contributions on the bottles, in µmol kg⁻¹: salinity 60.1, location 10.8, nitrate 6.1, sea surface height 6.0, silicate 4.6, temperature 3.9, phosphate 1.8, bottom depth 1.4 and chlorophyll 1.3. The maps below show the same contributions across the ocean, on a 1° grid and averaged over four seasonal dates in 2019. Unlike the sensitivity maps above, they describe the model's estimate at each place, not its response to a nudge.

blocks.note: Colour: contribution to the median estimate (µmol kg⁻¹) relative to the average over the ocean cells, ordered by mean |contribution|; each map has its own scale (±98th percentile). Hover or tap a map to read values; the ring marks the same place on every map.

ui.aria: Contribution of {name} to the estimated alkalinity

sections.title: Where predictors act together
sections.lead: Two predictors interact when the effect of one depends on the other. Salinity and location interact most strongly: the alkalinity–salinity slope differs between regions.

blocks.body: Two predictors interact when the effect of one depends on the other. The first figure shows the strength of each pair, as the mean absolute SHAP interaction value, with the main effect of each predictor on the diagonal. The strongest interaction is **salinity × location (11.8)**: the alkalinity–salinity slope differs between regions. Next come salinity × nitrate (3.8), temperature × silicate (3.0) and nitrate × silicate (2.4). For four pairs, the second figure shows the joint partial dependence on a 20 × 20 grid, and the pure interaction left over once the two single effects are subtracted. H² is the share of the joint effect's variance that this interaction explains: 0.465 for temperature × silicate and 0.458 for nitrate × silicate, but only 0.013 for salinity × nitrate and 0.003 for salinity × sea surface height, where the large salinity effect dominates the variance.

blocks.note: Matrix: click an outlined cell to open that pair below. Surfaces: partial dependence averaged over 400 bottles, each predictor spanning its 2nd to 98th percentile. Use "Interaction only" to see what the sum of the single effects does not explain.

ui.matrix_legend: Off-diagonal: interaction strength, µmol kg⁻¹ (square-root colour scale). Diagonal: main effect. Outlined cells open a surface below.
ui.pair_sub: H² = {h2}: {pct}% of the joint effect's variance is not the sum of the two single effects
ui.interaction_caption: Pure interaction, µmol kg⁻¹ (red above, blue below the sum of the single effects)

blocks.title: How to read these figures
blocks.body: The SHAP values use the path-dependent TreeSHAP algorithm. Correlated predictors, such as temperature and nutrients, share credit in ways that depend on how the trees split, so a contribution is not a causal effect of that predictor. Contributions are relative to the average estimate, not to zero. Interaction values cover only the boosted part of the model: the linear salinity baseline has no interactions by construction, so its slope varies with location only through the boosted residual.

sections.title: How the total uncertainty is built
sections.lead: The ensemble gives three variance terms: which data a model saw, which near-optimal model it is, and how wide its own predicted quantile band is.

items.title: Between data splits
items.body: Variance of the split means of the member medians: sensitivity to which cruises were seen.

items.title: Between near-optimal models
items.body: Mean within-split variance of member medians: hyperparameters, dropped features and refit randomness.

items.title: Predicted band width
items.body: Predicted Q90 − Q10 divided by 2.563, a normal-equivalent standard deviation (no normality is assumed).

sections.title: How the ensemble spread arises
sections.lead: Explore how the spread between members changes with which members are pooled.

sections.title: Uncertainty calibration
sections.lead: Does the predicted total uncertainty match the actual error on held-out data, and which terms make it up?

blocks.body: On the held-out test block the spread of member medians correlates with the absolute error at **r = {{spread_vs_error.corr_abs_err.member_std|2}}**, versus **r = {{spread_vs_error.corr_abs_err.scaled_iqr|2}}** for the scaled quantile width.

blocks.title: Read this as a ranking, not an error bar
blocks.body: Assess both the magnitude and ranking of uncertainty on held-out data. Member spread is not calibrated to prediction error.

comparison.title: What CARIMED and gridded salinity change
comparison.hero: What do Mediterranean CARIMED bottles and training on gridded instead of in-situ salinity change in the surface total alkalinity (TA) reconstruction? Three quantile-ensemble models are compared. Errors are predicted minus observed, in µmol kg⁻¹; MAE is the headline metric because the models are trained on the median.

C.name: GLODAP
C.desc: GLODAPv2.2023 bottles, trained on in-situ salinity. The baseline: no Mediterranean (CARIMED) data.

D.name: +MED
D.desc: +MED = GLODAP plus 1,205 Mediterranean CARIMED bottles; salinity predictor still in situ. Isolates what the extra Mediterranean data does.

E.name: +Grid-Sal
E.desc: Grid-Sal = trained on gridded salinity. Same bottles as +MED, but the salinity predictor is the gridded stack ESA CCI → SODA → multi-obs, i.e. what the maps see. This is the published model.

C·insitu.label: GLODAP · in-situ S input
C·insitu.desc: The GLODAP model scored with each bottle's in-situ salinity, the input it was trained on.

C·stacked.label: GLODAP · gridded S input
C·stacked.desc: The GLODAP model (trained on in-situ salinity) fed the gridded salinity stack, as it would be on the maps.

D·insitu.label: +MED · in-situ S input
D·insitu.desc: The +MED model scored with in-situ salinity: what in-situ input would give it.

D·stacked.label: +MED · gridded S input
D·stacked.desc: The +MED model (trained on in-situ salinity) fed the gridded salinity stack. The like-for-like reference for +Grid-Sal.

E.label: +Grid-Sal
E.desc: The +Grid-Sal model, trained and scored on the gridded stack. The published model.

mae.label: MAE
mae.tip: Mean absolute error of the median prediction. The headline metric, because the models are trained on the median. Lower is better.

rmse.label: RMSE
rmse.tip: Root mean squared error. Penalises large misses more than MAE. Lower is better.

bias.label: Mean bias
bias.tip: Mean of predicted minus observed. Closer to 0 is better; negative means under-prediction.

medbias.label: Median bias
medbias.tip: Median of predicted minus observed; robust to outliers. Closer to 0 is better.

r2.label: R²
r2.tip: Share of the variance in observed TA explained by the prediction. Higher is better (1 is perfect).

crps.label: CRPS
crps.tip: Continuous ranked probability score of the quantile forecast; rewards predictions that are both accurate and sharp. Lower is better.

cov80.label: 80 % coverage
cov80.tip: Share of observations inside the q10–q90 interval. Nominal 0.80: closer to 0.80 is better; lower means intervals are too narrow.

width.label: Interval width
width.tip: Mean width of the q10–q90 interval. Narrower is sharper, but only useful while coverage stays near 0.80.

calib.label: Calib. MAE
calib.tip: Mean absolute gap between nominal and observed coverage across the quantiles. Lower is better.

comparison.overview_intro: Each model differs from the previous one in exactly one thing. All numbers on this tab are held-out MAE on the same GLODAP rows, each row predicted only by ensemble members that never trained on it.

edges.label: salinity predictor: in situ → gridded stack

effects.label: overall MAE vs in-situ S input

comparison.test_note: The three models do not share one test block: GLODAP has 4,139 test rows, the other two 4,314 (only 332 shared). The held-out comparison removes this difference by scoring every row only with members that never trained on it.
comparison.limitations_title: Limitations shared by all three models
limitations: Intervals are too narrow. The nominal 80 % q10–q90 interval covers 70–74 % of held-out rows at best, and about 40 % when GLODAP or +MED are fed gridded salinity.
Coastal water is harder. Held-out MAE on coastal rows (bottom depth < 500 m) is 23–24 µmol kg⁻¹ with in-situ salinity input against 6–7 offshore; with gridded salinity input it is 42–55.
Fresh water and high latitudes. Below in-situ salinity 30, MAE is 42–44 with in-situ input and 88–99 with gridded input; |lat| ≥ 60° is the worst latitude band for every variant.

Gridded salinity dominates map error. Feeding gridded instead of in-situ salinity roughly doubles MAE for the models trained on in-situ salinity (10.0 → 25.0 for GLODAP, 9.7 → 25.6 for +MED on identical rows). Training on the stack recovers part of it (19.1) but does not close the gap.
comparison.heldout_intro: Every observation is scored only by members that never saw it: the test block by all 42 members, every other row by the 7 members of the split that held it out (median across members). "In-situ S input" scores a model with each bottle's own salinity; "gridded S input" feeds it the gridded stack (ESA CCI → SODA → multi-obs), which is what the maps see. The CARIMED effect is GLODAP → +MED at the same input; the gridded-training effect is +MED · gridded S input → +Grid-Sal.
comparison.heldout_loc_note: Hover or click a bar or chip to highlight that group. Points are a sample of 6,000 distinct sampling locations.
comparison.scatter_title: Predicted vs observed, test block sample
comparison.map_intro: Held-out residuals binned to 5° cells (cells with ≥ 5 rows). The difference views show where the chosen variant beats the reference: blue cells have a lower error than the reference.

The x-axis is fixed for each metric so bars stay comparable when you switch product, rows or models. +Grid-Sal has no in-situ-salinity score in the saved data, so its solid bar is its native (stack) score. Click a model in the legend to hide or show it.

Each point is the RMSE increase when a model is fed that product instead of in-situ salinity. A steep rise means the model is sensitive to salinity errors. +Grid-Sal is trained on the stack, so with the stack product all its rows have no mismatch; pick another product to compare it. n is the number of +MED test rows in each bin.

Held-out predictions use median aggregation (validation.yaml); the test-block table uses the saved mean aggregation. Basins are coarse boxes: Mediterranean 30–46° N, 5.5° W–37° E; Southern Ocean south of 35° S; Arctic/subpolar N north of 60° N; Indian 20–120° E north of 35° S and south of 30° N; Atlantic 70° W–20° E; Pacific otherwise.

questions.title: What does adding CARIMED do?

headline.label: Mediterranean MAE, µmol kg⁻¹ (gridded salinity input; GLODAP rows in the Mediterranean)

questions.answer: It fixes the Mediterranean, where GLODAP alone has almost no bottles to learn from, and leaves the rest of the ocean essentially unchanged.

questions.title: What does training on gridded salinity do?

headline.label: Overall MAE, µmol kg⁻¹, when predicting from gridded salinity (what the maps see)

questions.answer: A model that learns from gridded salinity copes better with its errors, and its 10–90 % intervals become far better calibrated. In-situ salinity would still give about half the error: gridded salinity remains the largest error source.

evaluation.title: Evaluation · HighresTA
evaluation.heading: Evaluation of the gridded-salinity model
evaluation.hero: How well the published model (trained and scored on the gridded salinity stack) reproduces bottle total alkalinity it has not trained on, by region, ocean basin, salinity and period.
evaluation.intro: Every row here is held out: the test block plus the out-of-fold rows of each split, pooled. Scores compare the median (q50) prediction with the bottle value. Click a row or a chip to see where its samples are; hover to preview.
evaluation.map_note: Orange dots are the held-out samples of the selected group (drawn from a random subset of 6,000 held-out rows).

group_note.valregion: Switch on any combination: deep or coastal ocean (500 m depth) and high (|lat| > 60°) or mid and low latitude; both or neither of a pair means no restriction. The Mediterranean (from the basin table) has no depth or latitude split, so it excludes the other switches. Excl. Mediterranean combines with them: alone it is exact (the other basins pooled), with a depth or latitude switch it is an estimate that removes the Mediterranean's share of the selection (its overall scores, apportioned by where its sampled points fall).
group_note.basin: Ocean basins as in the Held-out comparison tab.
group_note.salbin: Bins of the bottle's in-situ salinity.
group_note.year: Five-year periods, labelled by their first year.

evaluation.footnote: Bias is predicted minus observed, in µmol kg⁻¹; negative means under-prediction. Region scores pool the test block and out-of-fold rows exactly (from their MAE, RMSE and bias); the other groupings come from the pooled held-out table.
